title: Birthday Problem: Tight Collision Asymptotics
description: Proves the asymptotic upper bound for the birthday collision probability: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)). Fully proved from Mathlib with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, using the fundamental inequality 1-x ≤ exp(-x) and Gauss's summation formula.

originalContributions: Birthday collision upper bound: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)) (fully proved)
Collision probability lower bound: P(collision) ≥ 1 - exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)) (fully proved)

overview.historicalContext: The birthday problem was first posed by Richard von Mises in 1939 and popularized by mathematical recreationists. The exponential approximation $P \approx 1 - e^{-k^2/(2d)}$ became central to cryptography after Yuval (1979) showed that birthday-style attacks reduce the cost of finding hash collisions from $O(2^n)$ to $O(2^{n/2})$. The underlying inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$, a consequence of the convexity of the exponential function, was known to Euler and appears in Cauchy's 1821 Cours d'Analyse. This formalization makes the one-sided bound rigorous: the exact collision probability is always at least as large as the exponential approximation predicts, a fact implicitly assumed in security proofs for hash functions, digital signatures, and pseudorandom generators.
overview.problemStatement: Prove: $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (1 - i/d) \le \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d))$ for $k \le d$, and derive the collision lower bound $P(\text{collision}) \ge 1 - \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d))$.
overview.text: Proves the asymptotic upper bound for the birthday collision probability: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)). Fully proved from Mathlib with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, using the fundamental inequality 1-x ≤ exp(-x) and Gauss's summation formula.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof proceeds in three stages. First, apply the fundamental inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ to each factor $(1 - i/d)$ and use `Finset.prod_le_prod` to lift the pointwise bound to the full product. Second, collapse the product of exponentials $\prod e^{-i/d}$ into a single exponential $\exp(-\sum i/d)$ via `Real.exp_sum`. Third, evaluate the sum $\sum_{i<k} i/d = k(k-1)/(2d)$ using the Gauss summation formula proved by induction. Taking complements yields the collision lower bound.
keyInsights: The inequality $1-x \le e^{-x}$ (convexity of exp at its tangent line through the origin) is the single analytic fact that powers the entire bound
The Gauss sum $\sum_{i<k} i = k(k-1)/2$ gives the birthday bound its characteristic quadratic scaling $k \sim \sqrt{d}$, which is why birthday attacks achieve the square-root barrier
The threshold characterization $k(k-1)/(2d) > \ln(1/(1-p))$ explains the exact constant: for 50%, $23 \times 22 = 506 > 2 \times 365 \times \ln 2 \approx 505.97$
The bound is one-sided (upper on distinct, lower on collision) — the matching lower bound requires a second-order correction $O(k^3/d^2)$ from the Taylor remainder of $\ln(1-x)$
Monotonicity of collision probability is a simple consequence of each new factor being at most 1, but it establishes the intuitive fact that more people can only increase collision likelihood

sections.title: Probability Definitions
sections.summary: Defines probAllDistinct as the product ∏(1 - i/d) and probCollision as its complement, generalizing the birthday problem to arbitrary d.

sections.title: The Fundamental Inequality
sections.summary: Proves 1 - x ≤ exp(-x) for all real x via Mathlib's add_one_le_exp, the key analytic workhorse of the entire bound.

sections.title: Factor Nonnegativity and Boundedness
sections.summary: Establishes 0 ≤ 1 - i/d ≤ 1 for valid indices, the preconditions needed for Finset.prod_le_prod.

sections.title: Product-to-Exponential Bound (Sum Form)
sections.summary: The central technical step: lifts the pointwise inequality through the product and collapses via exp_sum to obtain ∏(1-i/d) ≤ exp(-∑ i/d).

sections.title: Gauss Summation Formula
sections.summary: Proves ∑_{i<k} i/d = k(k-1)/(2d) by induction, giving the closed-form exponent.

sections.title: Main Asymptotic Bound
sections.summary: Combines the product-to-exponential bound with Gauss's formula to prove P(all distinct) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2d)).

sections.title: Collision Probability Lower Bound
sections.summary: Takes the complement to obtain P(collision) ≥ 1 - exp(-k(k-1)/(2d)), the form used in cryptographic security analysis.

sections.title: Base Cases
sections.summary: Verifies boundary conditions: k=0 and k=1 give P(all distinct) = 1 and P(collision) = 0.

sections.title: Probability Validity ([0,1] Containment)
sections.summary: Proves P(all distinct) and P(collision) lie in [0,1], confirming the definitions are well-formed probabilities.

sections.title: Threshold Characterization
sections.summary: Proves that k(k-1)/(2d) > ln(1/(1-p)) guarantees P(collision) > p, explaining the 23-person threshold for d=365.

sections.title: Consistency with Parent File
sections.summary: Verifies definitional equality with the d=365 specialization in the parent birthday problem formalization.

sections.title: Monotonicity
sections.summary: Proves P(all distinct, k+1) ≤ P(all distinct, k): adding people can only increase collision probability.

conclusion.summary: Provides a complete formal proof of the birthday collision asymptotics with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The formalization covers the exponential product bound, collision lower bound, threshold characterization, monotonicity, and probability validity, all built from three key Mathlib results: add_one_le_exp, Finset.prod_le_prod, and Real.exp_sum.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: This bound underpins the security analysis of cryptographic hash functions: a hash with $n$-bit output requires only $O(2^{n/2})$ evaluations to find a collision (the birthday attack).

The formalization makes this reasoning machine-checkable, supporting verified cryptographic proofs. The threshold characterization also provides the exact constant for practical security parameter selection.
openQuestions: Can the matching lower bound $\prod(1-i/d) \ge \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d) - k^2(k-1)^2/(4d^2))$ be formalized using the second-order Taylor remainder of $\ln(1-x)$?
Can the Poisson approximation (the limit as $d \to \infty$ with $k^2/d \to \lambda$) be formalized in Lean, connecting to Mathlib's probability theory?
Can this be extended to the generalized birthday problem with $r$-way collisions, where the threshold scales as $d^{(r-1)/r}$?
